title: Lesson 2: Multi-Tenant Platform Architecture: Orgs, Environments, and the Instance Model
description: Why every Salesforce org rents a slice of a shared platform: multi-tenancy, metadata-driven design, the instance model, and the sandbox environments that keep Dev/QA/UAT/Prod safe.

questions.question: What does it mean that Salesforce is a multi-tenant platform?
options: Many tenants share one platform, with each org's data isolated.
Each customer gets a dedicated database server and its own schema.
Customers own the hardware their org runs on but share the license.
All tenants share one schema with no separation between records.
questions.explanation: Multi-tenancy means the platform runs many orgs on shared infrastructure, but each org's data is isolated by its OrgID.

questions.question: What is the guiding rule for arranging an environment ladder?
options: Every environment should hold a full copy of production data.
The production org doubles as the release rehearsal environment.
Each environment answers a question the one below it cannot.
Developer sandboxes are reserved for user acceptance testing.
questions.explanation: The ladder exists so each test question is answered by the cheapest environment capable of answering it, with a full copy reserved for release rehearsal.

questions.question: Why do governor limits push developers toward bulk, collection-based processing?
options: Because synchronous REST calls are always slower than asynchronous bulk calls.
Because limits cap per-transaction work to protect shared resources.
Because bulk processing always produces more accurate data.
Because small orgs are exempt from the platform's resource limits.
questions.explanation: Limits exist to keep one tenant from monopolizing shared resources, so code must process records in bulk within a single transaction budget.
